items.title: Rays rally in the 12th to keep World Series alive
items.summary: Trailing in the 12th inning of Game 4, Tampa Bay scored twice to beat Milwaukee 4–3. The Brewers still lead the Series 3–1, with Game 5 scheduled for tonight.

items.title: Arizona's newest national park has a volcanic origin
items.summary: NASA's Earth Observatory looks at Chiricahua National Park, where eruptions about 27 million years ago left rock that erosion sculpted into extraordinary spires and balanced formations.

items.title: Do spiders dream? Their sleep is surprisingly complicated
items.summary: Researchers studying jumping spiders observed two sleep stages, including REM-like eye movements and muscle twitches. The findings do not establish that spiders dream—but they do challenge simple assumptions about animal sleep.

items.title: One moon briefly disappears behind another
items.summary: NASA's astronomy picture for today shows Ganymede passing in front of Io. The rare mutual occultation is a reminder that Jupiter's moons put on their own celestial performances.

source.label: Source: NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day ↗

items.title: An ancient amphibian that lived at sea
items.summary: New fossils from roughly 237 million years ago point to an armored amphibian that may have spent its life in salt water—an unexpected evolutionary solution for animals whose skin generally presents challenges in marine environments.

items.title: How volcanoes built a landscape of stone towers
items.summary: The rock pinnacles at Chiricahua began with enormous volcanic deposits; weathering and erosion did the patient sculpting. NASA's satellite view reveals the larger landscape surrounding those formations.

items.title: Why Jupiter's moons sometimes eclipse each other
items.summary: The alignment needed to see one Galilean moon pass in front of another from Earth occurs around Jupiter's equinox. These events reveal how our viewing angle changes what we can observe.

deepDives.html:
Animal behavior · Paleontology · Evidence

When nature surprises us: what spiders and ancient amphibians teach us about evidence

What can a sleeping jumping spider and a fossil marine amphibian tell us about scientific discovery? Both stories remind us that unexpected evidence can challenge familiar assumptions—without answering every question.

This is an editorial connection between two independent research stories. The findings do not establish a biological link between spider sleep and ancient amphibians.

The surprising observations

Researchers studying the jumping spider Portia fimbriata reported behavioral evidence of two regulated sleep stages. One included eye movements and muscle twitches similar in appearance to REM sleep. That is intriguing, but it does not show that spiders experience dreams.

Separately, fossil discoveries in China point to Gerrothorax maritimus, an amphibian that apparently lived in Triassic seas about 237 million years ago. Its armor and other characteristics have prompted hypotheses about how it managed the challenges of salt water.

What the evidence can—and cannot—tell us

Spider researchers observed behavior and responses to disturbance; they did not directly measure dream experiences. Paleontologists interpreted anatomy, sediment context, and chemical evidence; they cannot watch the extinct animal swim. Each field asks questions that its available evidence can address.

The connection worth keeping

Discovery often begins when observations fail to fit our expectations. Good inquiry means following those clues while keeping claims within what the evidence supports.
